insider_note: The equation is already given as dy/dx = …, so there is no rearranging step here unlike some of the other homogeneous questions in this chapter — go straight to checking the degree and substituting y = vx.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: One mark. Every term is degree 2 in x and y, so the equation is homogeneous.
steps.memory_tip: y², xy and x² are all degree 2 — homogeneous of degree 2.
lines: Put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx
steps.why: Substituting y = vx into a ratio where every term of the numerator and denominator has the same total degree leaves the right side as a function of v alone, which is the test for a homogeneous equation.
common_mistakes: Cancelling x² incorrectly between the numerator and denominator.
Forgetting to replace dy/dx by v + x·dv/dx on the left before substituting on the right.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Subtract v as a fraction with denominator (1 − v).
steps.memory_tip: v(1 − v) = v − v² is the piece that combines with v² − 2v to give 2v² − 3v.
steps.why: Writing v as v(1 − v)/(1 − v) puts both terms over the same denominator; expanding v² − 2v − v + v² leaves 2v² − 3v, which is the function of v that separates from dx/x.
common_mistakes: Losing the −v term when expanding v(1 − v) = v − v².
Sign error combining v² − 2v − v + v² into 2v² − 3v.

steps.label: Write the partial fractions
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Factor the denominator 2v² − 3v as v(2v − 3) before splitting into partial fractions.
steps.memory_tip: 2v² − 3v = v(2v − 3) — a common-factor pull-out, not a two-bracket factorisation.
lines: and resolving into partial fractions gives A
steps.why: Splitting the fraction into a piece over v and a piece over (2v − 3) turns one hard integral into two easy ones, each matching a standard log-integral shape.
common_mistakes: Factoring 2v² − 3v as (2v − 1)(v − 3), which does not multiply back out correctly.
Solving for A and B with the wrong sign, since (1 − v) has a leading 1, not −v.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Both pieces give logs, but the second needs a compensating factor of 2 for its coefficient.
steps.memory_tip: ∫1/(2v−3) dv = (1/2)log(2v−3) — always divide by the coefficient of v inside the bracket.
steps.why: Each partial-fraction piece integrates by the standard rule ∫dv/v = log v, with a factor of 1/2 needed for the second term because its bracket has a coefficient of 2 in front of v.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the extra 1/2 factor needed when the bracket is (2v − 3) rather than (v − 3).
Losing the overall −1/3 factor shared by both terms.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Multiply by −3, exponentiate, then substitute v = y/x and clear every power of x.
steps.memory_tip: log(v√(2v−3)) = log(c/x)³ removes the fraction of logs in one multiplication by −3.
lines: ⇒ x⁶v²(2v − 3) = c⁶, and putting v = y/x:
steps.why: Multiplying by −3 clears the fraction of logs, exponentiating removes the log entirely, and substituting v = y/x with the matching power of x clears every fraction, giving the final whole-number relation with the constant relabelled.
common_mistakes: Squaring only the v√(2v−3) side and forgetting to square the c³/x³ side to match.
Losing a power of x when clearing v = y/x from inside the square root and the extra x³.
